chunks.raw_text: Multi-Modal Emotion Recognition (MMER) plays a crucial role in enhancing humancomputer interaction to interpret and respond to human emotions. While existing methods mostly rely on handcrafted features or simple feature concatenation, we introduce a new approach that refines multimodal fusion through cross-attention, enabling the learning of hierarchical dependencies directly from raw data. This allows for more effective interaction between modalities, improving emotion classification. We propose an MMER framework that integrates audio, text, and video modalities, leveraging deep learning models tailored to each data source. A cross-attention mechanism is employed to fuse information across modalities, ensuring the model focuses on the most salient emotional cues. Additionally, focal loss is used to address class imbalance, enhancing recognition of underrepresented emotional states. Evaluated on the IEMOCAP dataset, the proposed model achieves an average accuracy of 88.31% and an F1-score of 76.43%, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. These results demonstrate the system’s robustness in recognizing emotions in complex scenarios, highlighting its potential for real-world applications requiring accurate emotion assessment. The source code is avail[able at: https://github.com/alaaNfissi/Mental-Health-Monitoring-MMER.](https://github.com/alaaNfissi/Mental-Health-Monitoring-MMER)

chunks.raw_text: **Keywords:** Mutli-modal Emotion Recognition, Deep Learning, ALBERT, CNNs, Bi

MMER is gaining increasing attention due to its ability to integrate multiple data sources —audio, text, and video— to enhance the accuracy of human emotion analysis and interpretation. Emotion recognition plays a crucial role in human-computer interaction (HCI), where accurately detecting emotional states improves AI-driven user experiences and enables more effective support systems. Traditional unimodal emotion recognition approaches, which rely on a single modality such as speech, facial expressions, or text, show effectiveness but face major challenges in real-world applications. Their reliance on a single data source limits their ability to capture the full range of emotional cues, making them less robust in dynamic and complex environments [1–4]. Advancements in deep learning enable multimodal learning, which joins complementary information from different modalities to create a more comprehensive and robust emotion recognition system. Audio captures tone variations and speech patterns, video provides facial micro-expressions and non-verbal cues, and text offers rich semantic context. By using deep learning models for cross-modal fusion, MMER systems overcome the limitations of unimodal methods, allowing for more context-aware and robust emotion recognition [5–9]. MMER holds immense potential for mental health monitoring, particularly in detecting emotional distress for early intervention. Speech analysis serves as a key objective marker for detecting depression and suicidality [10]. Additionally, subtle cues in facial expressions and language patterns contribute significantly to psychological assessment. The ability of MMER systems to process these signals in real-time enhances their applicability in clinical

chunks.raw_text: MMER has seen significant advancements, driven by the availability of large-scale datasets and the rapid evolution of deep learning techniques. Early emotion recognition systems primarily relied on unimodal approaches, analyzing either speech [3], facial expressions [2], or text [18] independently. While these methods provided foundational insights, they struggled to capture the multidimensional nature of human emotions. This limitation led to the development of multimodal approaches, which integrate multiple data sources to enhance robustness and accuracy. A prominent area of research in MMER focuses on audio-video fusion, leveraging the complementary nature of these modalities. Studies such as [19] demonstrate that integrating audio and visual data significantly improves recognition performance. However, many of these early approaches relied on handcrafted features, such as Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) [20] for audio and facial landmarks for video. While effective, these manually engineered features limited the capacity of models to capture the full variability and depth of emotional expressions. More recent studies have explored advanced techniques, such as hierarchical attention for spectral analysis and multi-scale visual feature extraction

Nevertheless, the reliance on predefined features remains a bottleneck, restricting the ability to model the complex nuances of human emotions. The adoption of deep learning has addressed these challenges by enabling end-to-end feature extraction from raw data, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering. CNNs have proven highly effective in both audio and visual modalities. For instance, CNNs applied to raw speech waveforms capture subtle emotional cues without requiring heavy preprocessing [14]. Similarly, CNN-based models in video analysis extract meaningful facial expressions and visual patterns [9], traditional handcrafted methods by learning richer, high-level feature representations. Text-based emotion recognition has also benefited from advancements in transformerbased models. The ALBERT model, an efficient variant of BERT, has demonstrated strong performance in natural language processing (NLP) tasks [12]. By capturing deep semantic features, ALBERT enhances MMER systems’ ability to interpret linguistic context, leading to improved emotion classification accuracy. _Figure 1._ Architecture of the proposed multi-modal emotion recognition model.

chunks.raw_text: A key challenge in MMER lies in the effective integration of multiple modalities. Early fusion methods, which concatenate features at the input level, often fail to capture meaningful cross-modal interactions. To address this, recent attention-based fusion mechanisms, particularly cross-attention [16], dynamically allow modalities to influence each other by prioritizing the most relevant signals. This approach refines how multimodal data is processed and has been shown to improve MMER performance [21]. Despite these advancements, imbalanced datasets remain a persistent issue in deep learningbased MMER models. Standard loss functions tend to favor majority classes, leading to poor recognition of minority emotional states. To mitigate this, several techniques have been proposed, including alternative loss functions like focal loss [22], which assigns higher weights to underrepresented emotional categories, improving classification performance. To address these challenges, this work introduces a multi-modal emotion recognition framework that integrates audio, text, and video using CNNs, xLSTMs [15], ALBERT, and a cross-attention mechanism. Unlike earlier approaches that rely on handcrafted features, our system learns directly from raw data, leveraging CNNs for speech and video to capture high-level representations without manual preprocessing. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of early fusion techniques, our framework employs a cross-attention mechanism to refine interactions between modalities, ensuring that the model prioritizes the most relevant emotional signals. Additionally, to tackle class imbalance, we incorporate focal loss, which assigns greater importance to minority emotional categories, enhancing recognition performance across all emotional states. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves emotion recognition accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

chunks.raw_text: Human emotions are inherently multi-faceted, expressed through speech, facial expressions, and linguistic content. Each modality contributes distinct yet complementary information: text conveys semantic meaning and context, audio captures prosodic cues such as pitch, tone, and rhythm, and visual data provides non-verbal signals, including microexpressions and gestures. Relying on a single modality limits recognition accuracy, as environmental noise may distort speech, ambiguous phrasing can obscure textual sentiment, and occlusions or poor lighting can affect facial recognition. By integrating multiple modalities, our approach enhances robustness, compensates for the limitations of individual sources, and ensures a more holistic and reliable interpretation of emotions. _Figure 2._ Architecture of the audio modality.

triples.o: more holistic and reliable interpretation of emotions

chunks.raw_text: Our MMER system integrates three modalities—text, audio, and video—to improve emotion classification accuracy. As shown in Figure 1, the architecture consists of modalityspecific deep learning models, each tailored to extract high-level representations from its respective input. These representations are then fused using an advanced cross-attention mechanism, which dynamically prioritizes the most relevant emotional cues from each modality. This approach ensures optimal feature interaction and enhances the system’s ability to capture complex emotional states.

chunks.raw_text: Speech carries rich emotional information, conveyed through pitch, tone, and rhythm variations. Effectively capturing these cues requires modeling both local spectral features and long-term temporal dependencies. To achieve this, our approach integrates a CNN for hierarchical feature extraction from raw waveform inputs and a Bi-xLSTM to capture sequential dependencies. Unlike conventional methods that rely on handcrafted features or spectrogram-based representations, our model directly processes raw speech signals, allowing it to learn task-specific features adaptively, as illustrated in Figure 2. **CNN-Based Feature Extraction:** A given audio waveform, denoted as **x** audio _∈_ R _[T]_, where _T_ represents the sequence length, is processed through a series of convolutional layers. Our xLSTM implementation utilizes a 3M-LSTM in a bidirectional setting, allowing the model to process speech signals in both forward and backward directions. This bidirectional structure enhances contextual awareness by leveraging future and past acoustic information, enabling the network to extract fine-grained intonations, pauses, and rhythmic patterns essential for emotion detection. chunks.raw_text: The video modality processes facial expressions over time to extract meaningful emotional cues. To achieve this, our framework integrates three key components: MTCNN for face detection, RepVGG-CNN for feature extraction, and a Transformer Encoder for temporal modeling. This structured approach, illustrated in Figure 3, ensures robust emotion recognition by effectively capturing both spatial and temporal facial features. **MTCNN-Based Face Detection:** To achieve accurate face localization under various lighting conditions and orientations, we employ the Multi-Task Cascaded CNN (MTCNN) [24]. This approach localizes facial landmarks—including the eyes, nose, and mouth—using a three-stage pipeline:
_•_ P-Net (Proposal Network): Generates candidate face regions and their corresponding regression vectors.
_•_ R-Net (Refinement Network): Filters out false positives to refine the detected face regions.
_•_ O-Net (Output Network): Provides precise bounding box coordinates, confidence scores, and facial landmark detection.

By incorporating MTCNN, our model achieves high-accuracy face localization, even in the presence of occlusions or variations in scale. Once detected, faces are aligned and normalized before proceeding to the feature extraction stage. **RepVGG-CNN for Spatial Feature Extraction:** Following face detection, facial images are processed using RepVGG-CNN, a convolutional network designed for efficient and robust feature extraction. RepVGG [25] builds upon the VGG architecture [26] while incorporating structural re-parameterization, allowing the model to achieve faster inference while maintaining high accuracy. During training, RepVGG benefits from a multi-branch design, while at inference time, it transforms into a simple feedforward network for computational efficiency. Key components of RepVGG-CNN include:

chunks.raw_text: Class imbalance presents a major challenge in emotion recognition, where frequently occurring emotions (e.g., neutral, happy) dominate training distributions, leading to poor recognition of less common emotions (e.g., sad, angry). To mitigate this issue, our MMER model incorporates focal loss [22], an extension of cross-entropy loss designed to dynamically adjust the contribution of each sample based on its classification difficulty. Unlike standard loss functions that treat all samples equally, focal loss assigns a lower weight to well-classified instances while amplifying the contribution of harder-to-classify samples. This re-weighting mechanism ensures that minority class instances receive greater focus during training, improving their representation in the learned decision boundaries. The focal loss function is formulated as:

chunks.raw_text: The proposed method is evaluated on the widely used IEMOCAP dataset [17], a benchmark for MMER. This dataset comprises approximately 12 hours of audiovisual recordings, including speech, video, and transcriptions, making it well-suited for evaluating emotion recognition models across multiple modalities. For our work, we focus on four primary emotions distributed as in Figure 5: happy (excited), sad, angry, and neutral, as they are particularly relevant for distress detection. The dataset is partitioned into 80% for training, 10% for validation, and 10% for testing to ensure a robust and unbiased evaluation.

chunks.raw_text: Table 1 summarizes the classification performance across emotion categories. The model achieves an average accuracy of 88.31% and an F1-score of 76.43%, demonstrating strong generalization. For "Happy" it attains 87.55% accuracy, with a precision of 80.83%, recall of 78.96%, and an F1-score of 79.89%, showing a good balance between detection and false positives. In the "Sad" category, accuracy reaches 89.53%, with a recall of 76.21% but lower precision (70.09%), indicating some misclassifications. The F1-score of 73.02% reflects a reasonable trade-off. The model performs best in "Angry" recognition, achieving 91.34% accuracy and a high precision of 81.94%, though its recall (75.64%) is slightly lower, leading to an F1-score of 78.67%. The "Neutral" category shows good performance with 84.84% accuracy, but slightly lower precision (73.25%) and recall (75.08%), reflecting the challenge of distinguishing subtle neutral expressions. The F1-score of 74.15% indicates reliable classification. In Figure 6, the confusion matrix reveals the model’s classification performance. High recognition rates for happy (78.96%) and sad (76.21%) confirm its ability to capture emotional cues effectively. However, some misclassifications occur, particularly among overlapping emotions. Neutral expressions are sometimes misclassified as happy or sad due to subtle emotional undertones, while angry expressions occasionally appear as neutral or happy, likely due to shared facial and prosodic features. These findings highlight the complexity of emotional perception and the need for improved differentiation of subtle expressions.

chunks.raw_text: To assess the impact of key components in our model, we conducted two ablation studies. The first study examines the effect of the cross-attention mechanism and different modality combinations, while the second evaluates the effectiveness of Bi-xLSTM compared to TE architectures for capturing temporal dependencies. **First Study: Impact of Modality Combinations and Cross-Attention:** To analyze the role of different modalities, we evaluated their performance with and without the crossattention mechanism using the IEMOCAP dataset. Table 3 presents the results, demonstrating that integrating all three modalities (V+A+T) leads to better performance compared to two-modality combinations (V+T and A+T), which show lower accuracy and F1-scores. Moreover, incorporating the cross-attention mechanism consistently improves performance across all modality configurations. Notably, the V+A+T+cross setting achieves the highest accuracy (88.31%) and F1-score (76.43%), highlighting the benefit of cross-attention in enhancing multimodal fusion. These findings confirm that both multimodal integration and cross-attention play a crucial role in improving emotion recognition. **Second Study: Bi-xLSTM vs. TE for Temporal Modeling:** The second study evaluates the effectiveness of Bi-xLSTM compared to TE architectures for capturing temporal dependencies in speech signals. As shown in Table 4, Bi-xLSTM achieves the highest accuracy (88.31%) and F1-score (76.43%), consistently outperforming Transformer-based setups. In contrast, Bi-xLSTM, with its structured memory mechanism, is well-suited for sequential modeling, making it more effective for speech-based emotion recognition. Among the Transformer variants, the four-layer TE achieves the highest accuracy (86.78%), whereas increasing the number of attention heads (6 or 8) does not improve it. chunks.raw_text: This study presents an MMER system that integrates audio, text, and video modalities to improve emotion detection accuracy and robustness. Using cross-attention mechanisms and weighted fusion, the model dynamically prioritizes relevant information, achieving superior performance over SOTA methods on the IEMOCAP dataset. The results highlight the importance of multimodal fusion for capturing complementary emotional cues, particularly in mental health monitoring. A key strength of this approach is its cross-attention mechanism, which selectively integrates multimodal features. Additionally, the 3M Bi-xLSTM architecture, combined with CNN-based audio processing, effectively models sequential speech data, outperforming Transformer Encoder configurations in capturing long-range dependencies. These findings reaffirm the advantages of sequential modeling and convolutional processing for speech-based emotion recognition. Despite these improvements, challenges remain. The confusion matrix analysis shows misclassifications between closely related emotions, particularly sad and neutral, due to overlapping acoustic, visual, and textual features. Enhancing fine-grained feature extraction and cross-modal attention mechanisms could improve differentiation and synchronization of emotional cues. Expanding training data and incorporating data augmentation could also enhance generalization. Future work should focus on improving sensitivity to nuanced emotions by integrating speaker intent and conversational dynamics. Extending the model for real-time applications would enhance its utility in mental health, where emotion recognition supports early intervention. This underscores the potential of multimodal approaches in advancing emotion recognition and provides a foundation for future research on improving robustness, adaptability, and scalability.
